[[Category:Machine learning]]
[[Category:Large language models]]
A '''language model loss''' is the quantity minimised during training of a [[large language model (LLM)|language model]]: it measures how little probability the model assigns to the tokens that actually occur. In the notation of [[artificial neural network (ANN)|ANN]] training it is the '''cost function''' $C$ of the network. For a token sequence $x_1, x_2, \cdots, x_T$ and model parameters $\theta$, the loss is the mean negative log-likelihood of the observed tokens,

$$
C(\theta)
=
-\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log P_\theta(x_t \mid x_{1:t-1}),
$$

where $P_\theta(x_t \mid x_{1:t-1})$ is the probability the model assigns to token $x_t$ given the tokens that precede it, so that a single training example $x$ contributes $C_x$.

== Units ==

The logarithm fixes the unit. The natural logarithm gives nats per token, and rescaling gives bits per token,

$$
\begin{cases}
C_{\text{nat}}(\theta) = -\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log P_\theta(x_t \mid x_{1:t-1}) \\
C_{\text{bit}}(\theta) = \frac{C_{\text{nat}}(\theta)}{\ln 2}
\end{cases}
$$

Training reports conventionally quote $C_{\text{nat}}$.

== Perplexity ==

Perplexity is the exponential of the loss in nats,

$$
\operatorname{PP}(\theta) = \exp\big(C_{\text{nat}}(\theta)\big),
$$

and reads as the effective number of equally likely tokens the model is choosing between. A loss of $1$ nat per token therefore corresponds to a perplexity of $e \approx 2.718$.

== Relation to the pretraining objective ==

The loss is the negated, length-normalised form of the conditional log-likelihood that pretraining maximises,

$$
\log P_\theta(x_1, x_2, \cdots, x_T)
=
\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log P_\theta(x_t \mid x_{1:t-1})
=
-T\,C(\theta).
$$

Minimising the loss and maximising the likelihood are the same operation, and [[large language model (LLM)|scaling laws]] are stated in terms of the loss because it is the quantity whose behaviour is measured across model sizes.

== Irreducible loss ==

The loss is bounded below by the conditional entropy of the text itself: no model predicts next tokens better than the true distribution generates them. Scaling-law fits write this floor as $C_\infty$ and add reducible terms for the size of the model and for the size of the training set.<ref>{{#cite:Q3141}}</ref>

== Concrete examples ==

For a single predicted token the loss is $-\log P_\theta$, so it depends only on the probability the model gave the token that occurred:

{| class="wikitable"
|+ Loss of a single predicted token
! $P_\theta$
! $C_{\text{nat}}$
! $C_{\text{bit}}$
! $\operatorname{PP}$
|-
| $0.9$
| $0.105$
| $0.152$
| $1.11$
|-
| $0.5$
| $0.693$
| $1$
| $2$
|-
| $10^{-2}$
| $4.61$
| $6.64$
| $10^{2}$
|-
| $10^{-5}$
| $11.5$
| $16.6$
| $10^{5}$
|}

A model that is uniform over a vocabulary of $10^{5}$ tokens, that is $P_\theta = 10^{-5}$ for every token, therefore sits at $11.5$ nats per token, the no-knowledge baseline against which trained models are compared. Averaging over a sequence mixes such terms: a 2-token sequence predicted at $P_\theta = 0.9$ and then at $P_\theta = 0.5$ has a loss of

$$
C
=
-\frac{1}{2}\left(\log 0.9 + \log 0.5\right)
\approx 0.399 \text{ nats}
\approx 0.576 \text{ bits}.
$$

== Scaling of the loss ==

Empirically the loss falls as a power law in training compute $F$, measured in floating-point operations,

$$
C(F)=aF^{-\alpha},
\qquad \alpha \approx 0.05.
$$

The exponent governs how expensive further improvement is: halving the loss requires roughly $10^{6}$ times more compute, which is why the gap between $2$ nats per token and $1$ nat per token, a perplexity fall from $7.389$ to $2.718$, is very large in practice.<ref>{{#cite:Q3141}}</ref>
